newsitem.title: USA: Swollen rivers keep California on flood alert.
newsitem.headline: Swollen rivers keep California on flood alert.

text.p: Swollen rivers and shaky levees kept parts of California on flood alert on Wednesday as damage estimates from the devastating New Year flood passed $1.5 billion.

A voluntary evacuation was under way in the Weston Ranch area of Stockton, 60 miles (100 kms) southeast of San Francisco, because of potential problems with levees on the San Joaquin River, police said.
"If those levees failed the water has the potential to come into the Weston Ranch area," but there was no flooding yet, Stockton police spokesman Ken Praegitzer said.

Police went from door to door advising the area's 4,000 residents of the voluntary evacuation. Praegitzer did not know how many people chose to leave. "There are people leaving. We've had reports of people that are loading up furnishings and personal items," he said.

Another 4,000 people were advised to evacuate on Tuesday from near the town of Manteca in central California after two levee breaks on the San Joaquin River flooded a mobile home park and thousands of acres of farmland.
Officials say the New Year floods are almost certain to be the most costly in California history, surpassing the $1.8 billion of losses suffered in severe 1995 floods.

Damage to homes and businesses, roads and bridges has already passed $1.5 billion in just 19 of the 42 counties where Gov. Pete Wilson declared a state of emergency due to the floods and the final figure is sure to rise sharply.
The California floods have killed six people, damaged thousands of homes and inundated tens of thousands of acres of prime farmland.

President Bill Clinton has declared a major disaster in parts of California and areas of Idaho and Nevada that were also badly hit by punishing storms and floods. Oregon and Washington state also suffered heavy damage.
Farmers in California's fertile central valley have been hard hit, losing cattle and property, but the state said it was too early to estimate losses to the state's $22 billion farm industry.

The California Farm Bureau Federation said flood damage could affect farms for months to come as farmers coped with damage to buildings, land and equipment. But the federation said the timing of the storms may lessen crop damage because many crops had not yet been planted and grapevines and fruit and nut trees were in their winter dormancy stage.
The National Weather Service issued a flood warning for the San Joaquin and Tuolumne rivers in central California and a flash flood watch for the Stockton area on Wednesday.

High water along the San Joaquin River and some of the highest tides of the winter have raised concerns about levees along the river and the Sacramento-San Joaquin River delta, which flows out into San Francisco Bay. Workers feverishly reinforced levees in many areas.
"There's still a lot of levees being watched," California Office of Emergency Services spokesman Steve Martarano said.

Authorities reported on Wednesday that a few incidents of looting had taken place while thousands of people were evacuating from Marysville, 50 miles (80 kms) north of Sacramento, for several days last week.
